value: How the meanings of words change over historical time, measured computationally from text corpora.
Can word embeddings trained on successive historical periods quantify the statistical laws governing semantic change?
Uses diachronic word embeddings across centuries of text to quantify laws of semantic change (frequency and polysemy effects) - a landmark of computational digital humanities.

quote: We then apply this methodology in a large-scale cross-linguistic analysis using 6 corpora spanning 200 years and 4 languages (English, German, French, and Chinese).

Using six historical corpora spanning four languages and two centuries, we propose two quantitative laws of semantic change: (i) the law of conformity—the rate of semantic change scales with an inverse power-law of word frequency; (ii) the law of innovation—independent of frequency, words that are more polysemous have higher rates of semantic change.
Understanding how words change their meanings over time is key to models of language and cultural evolution, but historical data on meaning is scarce, making theories hard to develop and test.
